questions.q: You type `pokeapi.co` and press Enter. What happens first?
options: The browser sends its request for the page
A DNS lookup turns the name into an IP address
explanations: TLS needs a connection to run on, and a connection needs an address. It comes third.
The request is the last step. The browser can't send anything until it knows where to send it.
Right. Computers find each other by IP address, so the name has to become an address before anything else can happen.
TCP needs to know which address to connect to. It comes second, after DNS.
That's index `0`. Counting starts at zero.
Right. Splitting on `/` gives `['https:', '', 'pokeapi.co', 'api', ...]`. The empty string sits between the two slashes, so the host is at index `2`. It's the part DNS looks up.
`api` is at index `3`, after the host.
The empty string is at index `1`, between the two slashes of `://`.

questions.q: Two pieces of a response arrive in the wrong order, and one goes missing. What makes sure your code still gets all of it, in order?
options: Your code has to check for that itself
explanations: DNS only turns the name into an address. It's finished before any data moves.
Right. TCP numbers the data, re-sends what's missing and puts it back in order, so your code never sees the mess.
TLS keeps the data private and proves who the server is. Putting it back in order is TCP's job.
TCP handles it before your code ever sees the data.

options: An IP address for a name
Privacy, plus proof of who the server is
explanations: Turning a name into an address is DNS.
Reliable, ordered delivery is TCP's job.
Right. TLS encrypts the conversation, and the certificate proves the server is who it says it is.
TLS adds a handshake, so it doesn't make things faster. (HTTP/3 speeds up the setup by doing the connection and TLS together.)

questions.q: A login page loads over plain `http://`. It works fine. What's the problem?
options: There isn't one, as long as the page loads
The page will load more slowly
Nothing is encrypted, so someone on the same network may be able to see the password
explanations: Working isn't the same as being safe. That's exactly what makes plain HTTP dangerous.
Speed isn't the issue. Privacy is.
DNS looks up the name, not the scheme. It works the same for `http://` and `https://`.
Right. Without TLS, the password travels as plain text. On a shared network like café Wi-Fi, someone may be able to see it, or even change what you send.
